rows.source: HSE who should report under RIDDOR
rows.verified: RIDDOR reports should be submitted only by a responsible person with duties under the regulations.

rows.source: HSE who should report under RIDDOR
rows.verified: Responsible persons include employers, some self-employed people and those in control of work premises.
The responsible person selects and submits the appropriate online injury, dangerous-occurrence or disease form to the RIDDOR database.
Deaths, specified worker injuries, qualifying non-worker injuries and dangerous occurrences must be notified without delay, with the report received within 10 days.
Over-seven-day worker incapacitation must be reported within 15 days of the incident.
The over-seven-day period excludes the accident day but includes weekends, rest days and days the worker was not expected to work.
Over-three-day incapacitation remains subject to recording requirements even where the over-seven-day reporting threshold is not met.
A work-related non-fatal injury to a non-worker is reportable when it results in direct hospital treatment, subject to the regulation's scope.
A RIDDOR accident is a separate, identifiable and unintended incident that causes physical injury.
Non-consensual violence to a person at work is included within the RIDDOR accident definition.
Gradual cumulative exposure that eventually causes injury is not classed as an accident under RIDDOR, although a diagnosed occupational disease may fall under a different reporting route.
A reportable occupational disease requires a confirmed diagnosis by a doctor.
The diagnosed disease must be linked to exposure to a specified workplace hazard.
Dangerous occurrences are specified incidents with high potential to cause death or serious injury and are listed in Schedule 2.
Dangerous-occurrence reporting uses a reasonable judgement about whether the incident created a real risk of harm rather than requiring complex analysis.
HSE reported 126 workers killed in work-related accidents in 2025/26; the latest-year figure is provisional.
The provisional 2025/26 release recorded 25 construction deaths and 22 deaths in agriculture, forestry and fishing.
Falls from height accounted for 31 provisional worker deaths in 2025/26, around one quarter of the total.
Men accounted for 93% of provisional worker fatalities and workers aged 60 or over accounted for around one third.
HSE marks the most recent fatal-injury year provisional and finalises it a year later after late reports and quality checks; revisions are usually small but can vary.
